questions.question: Which among the following is exact opposite of inflation?
questions.explanation:
• Here the correct answer is option ‘D’.
  • Deflation is the situation where prices fall continuously or have tendency to fall whereas Inflation is sustained rise in the general level of prices of goods and services over time.
  • In this condition, the price level of goods and services decrease exponentially which results in an increase of the buying power of the money.

questions.question: What is creeping inflation?
options: Price increase at 3% or less in a year.
Price increases by more than 10% in a year.
Price increases by more than 50% in a month.
questions.explanation:
• Creeping or mild inflation is a stage where prices increase by 3% or less in a year. This inflation helps in the expansion of the economy as it boosts demand.

  • Walking inflation is a stage where prices increase between 3% and 10% in a year. It is harmful to the economy as the supply of goods can’t match up with the demand as people tend to buy more than they need to avoid higher prices in future.

  • Galloping inflation is a stage where prices increase more than 10% a year. It is disastrous for the economy as the money starts losing its value. Foreign investments dried up and the economy becomes unstable.

  • Hyperinflation is a stage where prices increase more than 50% in a month. It is a rare case and it erodes the real value of the local currency making people switch to a more stable currency. Zimbabwe experienced a 500 billion % inflation rate in 2008 where US$ 1 was equal to Z$ 2,621,984,228.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:

It is used to describe situations where the prices of all goods and services rise uncontrollably over a defined time. In other words, it is known as the extremely rapid inflation. This type of inflation occurs when the prices of goods and services rise more than 50% per month.

The above statements refer to which of the following type of inflation?
questions.explanation:
• Hyperinflation is a situation where the prices of all goods and services rise uncontrollably over a defined time. It is termed as the extremely rapid inflation.
  • It occurs when the prices of goods and services rise more than 50% per month and is considered as the last stage of inflation.

questions.question: The rates are decided by the central bank on the basis of the ________ in the market of the country.
questions.explanation:
• The rates are decided by the central bank on the basis of the inflation or recession in the market of the country.
  • When the market is hit by inflation, RBI increases the repo rate.
  • An increased repo rate denotes that the banks who borrow money during this period from the central bank will have to pay higher interest.

questions.question: The situation of rising prices combined with falling growth and employment is called _____.
questions.explanation:
• An economic cycle with slow growth, and high unemployment, combined with higher-than-normal inflation is termed stagflation.
  • Stagflation is difficult to handle as an attempt to correct one factor (unemployment or inflation) leads to the worsening of another.
  • Cosh-push inflation could lead to a situation of stagflation.

questions.question: Which of the following are the factors responsible for the cost-push inflation?
questions.explanation:
• Cost-push inflation is the decrease in the aggregate supply of goods and services stemming from an increase in the cost of production.
  • Increase in indirect taxes like custom and excise duty raise the cost of production increasing the price.
  • Apart from this, MSP (Minimum Support Price) increase and Infrastructural issues can also cause cost-push inflation.

questions.question: What is the impact of devaluation on inflation and economic growth?
options: It can decrease inflation and increase economic growth
It can increase inflation and decrease economic growth
It has no impact on inflation and economic growth
It can increase inflation and increase economic growth
questions.explanation:
• The impact of devaluation includes a decrease in the value of the domestic currency compared to other currencies, cheaper exports for domestic consumers, which discourages imports and reduces the current account deficit.

  • However, devaluation can also increase inflation and slow economic growth by raising the price of imports and increasing demand for domestic products.

  • Moreover, it can be perceived as a sign of economic weakness that could undermine investor confidence.

questions.question: When prices rise in a market where there is no control on prices by the government or any authority, then such inflation is known as ___________.
questions.explanation:
• Open Inflation occurs when the government and the monetary authorities of a country do not take any measure to control the spending of the people.
  • In this, there are no checks or controls on the distribution of commodities by the government.
  • Increase in demand and shortage of supplies persists which tend to lead to open inflation.
  • Unchecked open inflation leads to hyper-inflation.

questions.question: Which of the following is the base year of CPI for Industrial Workers (IW)?
questions.explanation:
• 2016 is the base year of the CPI for Industrial Workers (IW).
  • Consumer price indices are calculated in India: CPI for Industrial Workers, CPI for Agricultural Labourers, CPI for Rural Labourers, and CPI for Urban Non-Manual Employees.

questions.question: Which of the following rates measures the rise in prices of everything except food and energy?
questions.explanation:
• Core inflation measures the rise in prices of everything except food and energy, and such a measure is used because the prices of food and energy prices are very volatile.
  • Core inflation is used to show a long-run trend in the price level.

questions.question: When creeping and walking inflation are left unchecked, the rate of inflation will rise above 10% and it is termed as _________.
questions.explanation:
• When creeping and walking inflation are left unchecked, the rate of inflation will rise above 10% and hence, is termed as galloping inflation.
  • Galloping inflation is one that develops at a fast pace, but only for a brief period.
  • This form of inflation is dangerous for the economy as it mostly affects the middle and low-income classes of population.
  • It has the potential to trigger an economic downturn.

questions.question: Which of the following products has biggest basket in the wholesale cost index in India?
questions.explanation:
• The biggest basket of Wholesale Price Index is Manufactured Goods. It spans across manufactured products such as Textiles, Apparels, Paper, Chemicals, Plastic, Cement, Metals, and more.
  • It makes up 65% of the weight of the basket used in the Wholesale Price Index. Primary Articles like food make up to around 20% of the weight, and Fuel and Power make up to 1% of the weight.

questions.question: What is inflation?
options: Increase in the purchasing power of money
Decrease in the general price level of goods and services
Sustained rise in the average price level of goods and services
questions.explanation:
• Here, option ‘C’ is the correct answer.
  • Inflation refers to a sustained increase in the average price level of goods and services over time.
  • It represents a decrease in the purchasing power of money, meaning that the same amount of money buys less today than it did in the past.
  • The rate of inflation is typically expressed as an annual percentage and is often measured by government agencies, such as the consumer price index (CPI).
  • Factors such as changes in supply and demand, government policies, and global market conditions can influence inflation rates.

questions.question: Which of the following is a measure of inflation?
questions.explanation:
• The GDP deflator is also known as the implicit price deflator, and it is a measure of inflation.
  • It is defined as the ratio of the value of goods and services an economy produces in a particular year at current prices (GDP at current prices) to that of prices in the base year (GDP at base year prices).
  • GDP at current prices is called nominal GDP, while GDP at base year prices is called real GDP.
  • This ratio helps show the extent to which the increase in GDP is on account of higher prices than an increase in output.

questions.question: Which of the following is the term used for the amount through which actual aggregate demand falls short of aggregate supply at level of full employment?
questions.explanation:
• Deflationary Gap is the amount by which actual aggregate demand falls short of aggregate supply at level of full employment.
  • It leads to a fall in the price level.
  • It causes deflation and decreases wages and price level in the economy.
  • If an economy experiences a deflationary gap, then it will lead to rise in unemployment, and low/negative rates of economic growth.

questions.question: Which of the following method has been adopted by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) as the key measure of inflation?
questions.explanation:
• Reserve Bank of India had adopted the new Consumer Price Index (CPI) (combined) as the key measure of inflation in April 2014.
  • The national CPI is meant to measure retail inflation.
  • This index combines urban and rural CPIs, both under preparation and to be released simultaneously.
  • India does not have a unified CPI and uses the WPI as a benchmark.

questions.question: How many Consumer Price Indices are calculated in India?
questions.explanation:
• Consumer Price Index measures retail inflation in the economy using the data related to the change in prices of most common goods and services used by consumers.
  • There are four types of CPIs in the country:
  1. CPI for Industrial Workers (IW) Base Year2
  2. CPI for Agricultural Labourers (AL)
  3. CPI for Rural Labourers (RL)
  4. CPI for Urban Non-Manual Employees (UNME)
  • CPI for Industrial Workers, Agricultural Labourers, and Rural Labourers are compiled by the Labour Bureau in the Ministry of Labour, while the CPI for Urban Non-Manual Employees is compiled by the Ministry of Statistics and Program Implementation.

questions.question: Which of the following terms is used to denote a situation of decrease in general price levels in an economy?
questions.explanation:
• The term deflation is used to refer to a situation of a decrease in the general price levels in the economy. In other words, it is the exact opposite of inflation.
  • For example, if the price of a basket of goods has fallen from Rs 100 to Rs 80, it’s a reduction in the overall prices of goods, and thus, termed deflation.

questions.question: Who compiles the CPI for Urban Non-Manual Employees (UNME) in India?
questions.explanation:
• 4 consumer price indices are calculated in India: CPI for Industrial Workers, CPI for Agricultural Labourers, CPI for Rural Labourers, and CPI for Urban Non-Manual Employees

  • The CPI for Urban Non-Manual Employees is compiled by the National Statistical Office (NSO), which is under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation.

  • The other three consumer price indices are compiled by the Labour Bureau.

questions.question: Who compiles the CPI for Urban Non-Manual Employees (UNME) in India?
questions.explanation:
• Consumer price indices are calculated in India: CPI for Industrial Workers, CPI for Agricultural Labourers, CPI for Rural Labourers, and CPI for Urban Non-Manual Employees
  • The CPI for Urban Non-Manual Employees is compiled by the National Statistical Office (NSO), which is under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation.
  • The other three consumer price indices are compiled by the Labour Bureau.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a cause of inflation?
options: All of the above are causes of inflation
questions.explanation:
• The causes of inflation are:
  1. Demand-Pull Inflation is mainly due to an increase in Aggregate Demand (AD). The increase in AD can come from either an increase in Government Expenditure (Expansionary Fiscal Policy) or an increase in expenditure from Households and Firms.
  2. Cost-push Inflation occurs when the cost of production increases. There is an increase in the prices of the inputs, which increases the price of the products.
  3. Structural Inflation is due to bottlenecks like agricultural, Foreign Exchange, and Infrastructural. This type of inflation is prevalent in low-income countries and developing countries.
  4. An increase in money supply by the Central Bank can cause an increase in inflation by increasing demand in the economy.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements are correct with respect to Core Inflation?

  1. It is the change in the costs of goods and services and does not include food and energy sectors.
  2. It is considered as an indicator of long-term inflation.
  3. Core inflation is dominated by the transport and communication categories in India.

Choose the correct codes:
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer (A).

  • Core Inflation is measured as CPI inflation excluding food and fuel to avoid the impact of short-term volatility.

  • It is regarded as a long-term measure of underlying inflation trends, useful for monetary policy.

  • In India, core inflation is mainly influenced by housing, health, education, clothing, and other services.

  • Transport & communication has at times driven inflation spikes (e.g., telecom tariff hikes), but it is not structurally the dominant category.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of hyperinflation?
questions.explanation:
• Here the correct answer is option ‘C’.
  • An annual inflation rate of 50%, is an example of hyperinflation.
  • Hyperinflation is an extremely high and typically accelerating inflation.
  • It can cause a rapid loss of purchasing power and value of money.
  • One example of hyperinflation is the 1923 French franc collapse, when the franc lost nearly all its value due to the government printing excessive amounts of paper currency.
  • Another infamous example is the Zimbabwean dollar, which experienced multiple instances of hyperinflation in the 2000s, reaching record-breaking levels of 89.7 quadrillion percent in 2009.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between CPI and WPI?
options: CPI measures retail prices; WPI measures wholesale prices.
CPI includes only essential commodities; WPI includes all goods.
CPI tracks export prices; WPI tracks import prices.
CPI measures industrial prices; WPI measures service prices.
CPI excludes food items; WPI includes them.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer is CPI includes only essential commodities; WPI includes all goods.

CPI measures retail prices paid by consumers, while WPI focuses on wholesale prices at the producer level, primarily for bulk goods.

  • CPI (Consumer Price Index):

    • Measures the average change in prices of a basket of goods and services commonly consumed by households.  
       
    • Reflects price movements at the retail level – what consumers actually pay for goods and services.  
       

  • WPI (Wholesale Price Index):

    • Measures the average change in prices of goods sold in wholesale markets.  
       
    • Tracks price changes at the producer level – before goods reach the retail stage and are sold to consumers.  
       

Key takeaway: CPI focuses on what consumers pay, while WPI focuses on what businesses pay for goods before they reach the consumer market.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct in the context of inflation?
options: WPI is the key measure of inflation in India.
The core inflation measures overall inflation in the economy
Inflation benefits the debtors or the borrowers.
questions.explanation:
• CPI, Consumer Price Index, is the key measure of inflation in India.
  • The headline inflation measures the level of overall inflation in the economy, while the core inflation measure excludes the prices of food and fuel components as they are highly volatile.
  • Inflation benefits the debtors or the borrowers, as they have to pay less worth rupees due to inflation, while the creditors get a fixed rate of interest. Hence, this statement is correct.
  • The base year of the Wholesale Price Index is 2011-12.

questions.question: Which one among the following items has maximum weight in wholesale price index in India?
questions.explanation:
the specific weights assigned to various items in the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) in India can change over time due to updates and revisions by the statistical authorities. However, historically, the primary items that have had significant weights in the WPI basket include:

  1. Primary Articles: This category includes food articles, non-food articles, and minerals. Within this category, food articles, especially cereals, pulses, and vegetables, have often carried substantial weights.

  2. Fuel and Power: Items like petrol, diesel, electricity, coal, and other forms of energy contribute to this category.

  3. Manufactured Products: This includes a wide range of goods produced in the manufacturing sector. Various sub-sectors such as food products, textiles, chemicals, basic metals, machinery, etc., are part of this category.

The weightage is as follows: Manufactured Products (64.20%), Primary Articles (22.60%) and Fuel & Power (13.10%).

questions.question: Which of the following is the total inflation in an economy and includes inflation in a basket of goods that includes commodities like food and energy?
questions.explanation:
• Headline inflation is the total inflation in an economy and includes inflation in a basket of goods that includes commodities like food and energy.
  • Inflation rate expressed in Wholesale Price Index (WPI) usually denotes the headline inflation.

questions.question: Which of the following inflation related terms is not correctly given with its depiction?
options: Misery index: Rate of inflation + Rate of unemployment
questions.explanation:
• Repressed inflation is a situation in which price and wage increases are restrained by official controls.
  • Here, Aggregate demand > Aggregate supply.
  • Hence, E is the correct option.

questions.question: With reference to inflation in India, which of the following statements is correct?
options: Controlling the inflation in India is the responsibility of the Government of India only
The Reserve Bank of India has no role in controlling the inflation
Decreased money circulation helps in controlling the inflation
Increased money circulation helps in controlling the inflation
questions.explanation:
A decrease in money circulation, often achieved through monetary policy measures, can be a tool to help control inflation. Here's how:

  1. Reducing Aggregate Demand: When there is less money in circulation, consumers and businesses have less purchasing power. This reduction in aggregate demand can help prevent excessive demand for goods and services, which, if unchecked, could lead to inflationary pressures.

  2. Interest Rate Policies: Central banks can implement monetary policies, such as raising interest rates, to reduce the money supply and make borrowing more expensive. Higher interest rates can discourage spending and investment, leading to a decrease in aggregate demand.

  3. Controlling Credit: Central banks can also implement measures to control the availability of credit in the economy. By tightening credit conditions, they can reduce borrowing and spending, which helps in curbing inflation.

  4. Price Stability: Maintaining a stable and predictable level of prices is a key goal for central banks. By adjusting the money supply and interest rates, they aim to keep inflation within a target range to achieve price stability.

questions.question: A _____ inflation is the one ​​where inflation rises to 10% or more.
questions.explanation:
• When the inflation rate rises to 10% or more in a year, it is termed galloping inflation. It can wreak havoc on the economy as money loses its purchasing power quickly.
  • People cannot keep up with the costs and the prices, and foreign investors also avoid investing in that country.
  • Thus, in the case of galloping inflation, an economy becomes unstable. It, therefore, must be prevented.

questions.question: Which component has the highest weight in the CPI for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer is Food and Beverages.

The CPI for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW) in India gives the highest weight to Food and Beverages.

  • Essential Expenditure: Food is a fundamental necessity for survival. A significant portion of an industrial worker's income is spent on food and beverages.
  • Price Volatility: Food prices can be highly volatile, influenced by factors like weather patterns, supply chain disruptions, and global market fluctuations.
  • Impact on Household Budgets: Fluctuations in food prices directly impact the purchasing power and overall well-being of industrial workers and their families.

Therefore, the CPI-IW assigns a higher weight to Food and Beverages to accurately reflect its substantial impact on the living expenses of this specific demographic.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:

  1. Food
  2. Energy
  3. Leather products
  4. Financial Services
  5. Retail Services

Which of the items are excluded while measuring core inflation?
questions.explanation:
• Price rise in all goods and services except food and energy due to high prices fluctuations is core inflation.
  • It is calculated as government needs a stable and true picture of inflation.

questions.question: Which of the following indices does NOT include food and fuel in its calculation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer is Core CPI.

  • Core CPI excludes volatile components like food and fuel to focus on underlying inflation trends. 
  • Core CPI excludes volatile components such as food and fuel to provide a clearer view of underlying inflation trends. In contrast, headline CPI, WPI, and GDP deflator include these components in their calculations.

questions.question:
Consider the following statement about Stagflation:

  1. It is a situation in which the inflation rate is high, economic growth rate is slow, and unemployment remains steadily high
  2. It can be obtained from Philips curve
  3. It can occur, when central bank creates money flow by printing more currency but puts supply on hold.

Which of the following statements are correct?
questions.explanation:
• Stagflation is a situation in which the inflation rate is high, economic growth rate slows, and unemployment remains steadily high. It is also known as recession inflation.
  • It can occur, when a central bank creates money flow by printing more currency but puts supply on hold. It can also rise when the central bank's monetary or fiscal policies create credit.
  • Philips curve cannot explain stagflation.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct in the context of inflation?
options: WPI is the key measure of inflation in India.
The core inflation measures overall inflation in the economy.
Inflation benefits the debtors or the borrowers.
questions.explanation:
• CPI, Consumer Price Index, is the key measure of inflation in India.

  • The headline inflation measures the level of overall inflation in the economy, while the core inflation measure excludes the prices of food and fuel components as they are highly volatile.

  • Inflation benefits the debtors or the borrowers, as they have to pay less worth rupees due to inflation, while the creditors get a fixed rate of interest. Hence, this statement is correct.

  • The base year of the Wholesale Price Index is 2011-12.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements

  1. When prices of goods and services rise by more than 50% per month, it is known as hyperinflation.
  2. It is the last stage of inflation.
  3. It is also known as recession inflation

Which of the following statements are correct with respect to Hyperinflation?
questions.explanation:
• Hyperinflation is when the prices of goods and services rise more than 50% per month.
  • It is the last stage of inflation.
  • Examples: Germany in the 1920s, Zimbabwe in the 2000s, American Civil War and Venezuela in 2018.
  • Stagflation is known as recession inflation

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct in terms of the outcome of inflation?
options: Inflation leads to the depreciation of the currency of a country.
Due to inflation, exports are cheaper and imports are costlier.
questions.explanation:
• Due to inflation, there is a decrease in the purchasing power of a currency, which leads to the depreciation of that currency.
  • Due to depreciation, exports are cheaper and thus increase, while imports reduce.
  • Inflation benefits debtors and hurts the creditors as the interest rate is fixed. The debtors pay less in terms of real currency value, thus benefiting.

questions.question: The rate of inflation in India is measured generally in respect of movement of ______.
options: cost of living index for agricultural labour
questions.explanation:
In India, the rate of inflation is generally measured with respect to the movement of the Consumer Price Index (CPI). The CPI is a key indicator that reflects the average change in prices paid by urban and rural consumers for a basket of goods and services over time. The basket typically includes essential items such as food, clothing, housing, medical care, education, and other goods and services.

There are different variations of the CPI used in India to capture inflation for specific population groups and regions. For example:

  1. CPI for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW): Measures inflation for industrial workers and is used for the calculation of dearness allowance for government employees.

  2. CPI for Agricultural Labourers (CPI-AL): Measures inflation for agricultural laborers.

  3. CPI for Rural Labourers (CPI-RL): Measures inflation for rural laborers.

questions.question: _____ occurs when enough people expect inflation to continue in the future.
questions.explanation:
• A built-in inflation is a result of expectations of a rise in future prices
  • Due to these expectations in the economy, workers may end up demanding higher wages in order to maintain their standard of living.
  • Increased wages would result in increased costs for businesses, which pass those costs on to end consumers.
  • Hence, built-in inflation is also a cause of inflation and can be influenced either by demand-pull inflation or cost-push inflation.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a cause of inflation?
questions.explanation:
• The causes of inflation are:

  1. Demand-Pull Inflation is mainly due to an increase in Aggregate Demand (AD). The increase in AD can come from either an increase in Government Expenditure (Expansionary Fiscal Policy) or an increase in expenditure from Households and Firms.

  2. Cost-push Inflation occurs when the cost of production increases. There is an increase in the prices of the inputs, which increases the price of the products.

  3. Structural Inflation is due to bottlenecks like agricultural, Foreign Exchange, and Infrastructural. This type of inflation is prevalent in low-income countries and developing countries.

  4. An increase in money supply by the Central Bank can cause an increase in inflation by increasing demand in the economy.

questions.question: Which one of the following is not one of the primary goals of the Reserve Bank of India's monetary policy?
questions.explanation:
• The three primary objectives of the monetary policy are

(1) Price Stability or Control of Inflation,

(2) Economic Growth, and

(3) Exchange Rate Stability.

  • Monetary policy plays an important role in price stability [inflation control], economic growth, job creation, and social justice in any economy.

  • Monetary policy refers to credit control measures used by the central bank to regulate and control the level of credit creation by commercial banks.

  • Lack of credit facilities results in a fall in money supply and deflation or deficiency in demand in the economy. Monetary policy aims at controlling the excess or deficiency in demand

questions.question:
Which of the following statements is correct regarding Reverse Repo rate?

1. Reverse Repo Rate is used by bank when they have surplus funds

2. Reverse Repo rate earns income through lending to banks

3. Reverse Repo rate is used to control inflation
questions.explanation:
• The interest rate on commercial banks' deposits with the central bank is known as the reverse repo rate. In order to safeguard their funds in the case of an excess, the majority of banking institutions choose for this safer technique. The reverse repo rate is, in other words, an interest rate that is paid on deposited cash.
  • The repo rate and reverse repo rate are fundamentally different from one another because the repo rate generates income by lending to commercial banks, whilst the reverse repo rate generates income by paying interest on money deposited with the Reserve Bank of India.
  • Whereas the repo rate is used to manage inflation, the reverse repo rate is used to control the liquidity of the economy. Central banks always maintain the reverse repo rate lower than the repo rate.

questions.question: If the RBI raises the Cash Reserve Ratio, what will happen?
questions.explanation: • When CRR is increased , it decreases money supply, Increases interest rates on home loans, car loans etc. and in inter-bank market, Increases demand for money and decreases inflation.

questions.question: What is the main tool used by the RBI to control money supply in the economy?
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is B, that is Open market operations.
  • The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) uses a variety of monetary policy tools to control the money supply in the economy, including open market operations (OMOs), bank rate policy, and quantitative easing (QE).
  • OMOs involve buying and selling government securities in the secondary market to influence the money supply and interest rates.
  • The RBI may also adjust the bank rate, which is the interest rate at which the RBI lends to commercial banks, to either increase or decrease the demand for credit and thereby control the money supply.
  • QE, on the other hand, involves the creation of new money by the RBI to stimulate economic activity.

questions.question: Which of the following monetary policy objectives does not directly control, however, through the monetary policy?
questions.explanation:
• NBFIs or Non-Banking Financial Institutions like IDBI, UTI, IFCI, etc. play a vital role in the Indian economy.
  • They help in the deployment of credit and also the mobilisation of savings.
  • RBI does not directly control the functioning of these institutions.
  • However, the monetary policy can indirectly influence the policies and functions of the NBFIs.

questions.question: Who controls the Money Supply in India?
questions.explanation:
• In India, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) controls the money supply.
  • The RBI is an independent central bank that regulates monetary policy and manages the country's foreign exchange reserves.
  • The Indian government has given the RBI the power to issue currency and regulate the money supply to achieve specific economic goals such as price stability and economic growth.
  • The RBI uses various tools such as open market operations, repo rates, and monetary policy committees to control the money supply and manage inflation.

questions.question: In India, what is the statutory liquidity ratio (SLR) used for?
questions.explanation:
• Here, the correct answer is option ‘D’, that is Ensuring liquidity in the banking system.
  • The statutory liquidity ratio (SLR) is a regulatory requirement imposed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on commercial banks to maintain a minimum level of liquid assets in their reserves.
  • These liquid assets include cash, gold, treasury securities, and other marketable assets.
  • The SLR is used to ensure that banks have adequate liquidity to meet customer withdrawals and other short-term obligations.
  • It is also used by the RBI to manage monetary policy and control inflation
  • SLR is the percentage of total deposits that banks are required to maintain in the form of liquid assets, such as government securities.

questions.question: When did the Monetary Policy Committee come into being?
questions.explanation:
• It was the Urjit Patel Committee that first proposed the idea for the formation of a 5-member Monetary Policy Committee. The government later proposed the setting up of a 7-member committee.
  • The Monetary Policy Committee came into force in June 2016, and the first meeting was conducted in October 2016 in Mumbai.
  • It is constituted as per Section 45ZB under the RBI Act of 1934.

questions.question: If a bank fails to maintain the prescribed SLR, it is liable to pay a penalty to the RBI of ______ above the bank rate on the deficient amount for that particular day.
questions.explanation:
• Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) is a particular portion of the Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) that the commercial banks are required to maintain in the form of cash, gold, or other liquid assets by the end of the day.
  • The government uses the SLR to control inflation and increase economic growth. Increasing the SLR will control inflation in the economy, and decreasing the statutory liquidity rate will increase growth in the economy.
  • If a bank fails to maintain the SLR, it is liable to pay a penalty to the RBI. The bank which has defaulted has to pay a penalty of 3% above the bank rate on the deficient amount for a particular day.

questions.question: Which of the following is an instrument of the Monetary Policy Committee?
questions.explanation:
• The instruments of MPC are:

  1. Bank Rate: The rate at which the RBI lends money to commercial banks without any collateral or security. The bank rate is also the standard rate at which the RBI will buy or discount bills of exchange and other commercial instruments. An increase in this rate will reduce the money supply and vice versa.

  2. Cash Reserve Ratio: CRR is the portion of deposits that commercial banks have to deposit to the RBI. CRR is also a great tool to control inflation as an increase in this rate will reduce the money supply in the economy and vice versa.

  3. Statutory Liquidity Ratio: ​​It is the percentage of total deposits that commercial banks keep with themselves in form of cash reserves or gold.

  4. Repo rate: It is the interest rate at which the RBI provides overnight liquidity to banks against the collateral of government and other approved securities.

  5. Reverse Repo Rate: It is the interest rate at which the RBI absorbs liquidity from commercial banks on an overnight basis against the collateral of eligible government securities.

questions.question: The rate at which the RBI lends money to commercial banks for a short term (a maximum of 90 days) is called_____.
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'D' that is 'Repo rate'.
  • The Repo Rate is the rate at which the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) lends short-term funds to commercial banks, usually against the collateral of government securities.

Key Info: 

  • Tenure: Short-term, generally up to 90 days.

  • Purpose of Repo rate is to inject liquidity into the banking system when banks face a shortfall.

  • It is a monetary policy tool to control inflation and stabilize the economy.

Other related rates for clarity:

  • Reverse Repo Rate: The rate at which RBI borrows money from commercial banks.

  • Bank Rate: The rate at which RBI lends long-term funds (beyond 90 days) to banks.

questions.question: Which of the following is a collateral free agreement?
questions.explanation: • Standing Deposit Facility allows the RBI to absorb liquidity (deposit) from commercial banks without giving government securities in return to the banks.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)?

(i) It has the authority to decide repo rate, CRR, SLR

(ii) Its decision is not binding on RBI

(iii) The committee comprises 8 members

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
• The MPC has the authority to decide only the repo rate, not CRR & SLR or other things.

  • The MPC determines the repo rate, based on consumer price indices, and this rate is binding on the RBI, as per section 45ZB of the amended RBI Act.

  • This benchmark rate is the reference against which all other interest rates are decided in the country.

  • The committee comprises six members - three officials of the Reserve Bank of India and three external members nominated by the Government of India.

questions.question: How does an increase in the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) impact the banking system?
questions.explanation:
• Here, the correct answer is option (D) that is ‘Reduces liquidity in the banking system.’
  • When the CRR is increased, banks are required to keep a higher percentage of their deposits as reserves with the RBI, limiting the funds available for lending and investment, and thus reducing liquidity.
  • This leads to a reduction in the funds available with banks for lending and investment.
  • The increase in CRR results in a decrease in the money supply in the economy since a significant portion of the funds that banks would otherwise lend is now held as reserves with the central bank.

questions.question: Which of the following institution(s) qualifies to use the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) to borrow money from or park excess funds with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI)?
questions.explanation:
LAF is a facility extended by the Reserve Bank of India to the scheduled commercial banks (excluding RRBs) and primary dealers to avail of liquidity in case of requirement or park excess funds with the RBI in case of excess liquidity on an overnight basis against the collateral of Government securities including State Government securities.

  • Basically LAF enables liquidity management on a day to day basis.

questions.question: How many members are there in the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) from the RBI?
questions.explanation:
• ​The committee comprises six members - three officials of the Reserve Bank of India and three external members nominated by the Government of India.

  • The Monetary Policy Committee is responsible for fixing the benchmark interest rate in India.

  • The meetings of the Monetary Policy Committee are held at least four times a year (specifically, at least once a quarter) and it publishes its decisions after each such meeting.

  • The committee comprises six members - three officials of the Reserve Bank of India and three external members nominated by the government of India.

  • They need to observe a "silent period" seven days before and after the rate decision for "utmost confidentiality".

  • The governor of the Reserve Bank of India is the chairperson ex officio of the committee.

  • Decisions are taken by the majority with the governor having the casting vote in case of a tie. The current mandate of the committee is to maintain 4% annual inflation until 31 March 2026 with an upper tolerance of 6% and a lower tolerance of 2%.

questions.question:
Which one(s) of the following describes one(s) or more forms of external benchmark rates?

  1. Repo and Reverse repo rate.
  2. Financial Benchmarks India Private Ltd. publishes the yield on 3-Month Treasury Bills issued by the Indian government (FBIL).
  3. Financial Benchmarks India Private Ltd. publishes the yield on 6-Month Treasury Bills issued by the Indian government (FBIL).
questions.explanation:
• The RBI has made it compulsory for banks to link their new floating rate home, auto and MSME loans to an external benchmark so that the borrowers can enjoy lower rate of interest.
  • All new floating rate personal or retail loans (housing, auto, etc.) and floating rate loans to Micro and Small Enterprises extended by banks from October 01, 2019 shall be benchmarked to one of the following:
  1. Reserve Bank of India policy repo rate
  2. Government of India 3-Months Treasury Bill yield published by the Financial Benchmarks India Private Ltd (FBIL)
  3. Government of India 6-Months Treasury Bill yield published by the FBIL
  4. Any other benchmark market interest rate published by the FBIL.

questions.question: Which of the following is/are not the objective of Monetary Policy?
questions.explanation:
• The three objectives of monetary policy are controlling inflation, managing employment levels, and maintaining long-term interest rates.
  • Monetary policy is a central bank's actions and communications that manage the money supply.
  • Central banks use monetary policy to prevent inflation, reduce unemployment, and promote moderate long-term interest rates.

questions.question: What is the significance of the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) in India's monetary policy?
questions.explanation:
• Here, the correct answer is option C, that is Providing short-term liquidity to banks.
  • LAF allows banks to manage their day-to-day liquidity needs by borrowing or lending in the money market.
  • The LAF allows the RBI to provide short-term loans to commercial banks, which in turn can be used to make long-term investments or lend to other entities.
  • This process helps to ensure that there is sufficient liquidity in the banking system, which is crucial for economic growth.
  • Additionally, by allowing the RBI to control the money supply, the LAF helps to stabilize interest rates and inflation in the economy.

questions.question: How does the Liquidity Adjustment Facility impact short-term interest rates in the economy?
options: It has no effect on interest rates
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'D' that is 'It stabilizes interest rates'.
  • The Liquidty Adjustment Facility (LAF) has a direct impact on short-term interest rates. By adjusting the Repo and Reverse Repo rates, the RBI influences the cost of borrowing and lending in the money market, thereby affecting short-term interest rates.

Key Info: 

  • The Liquidity Adjustment Facility, through adjustments in the Repo Rate and Reverse Repo Rate, acts as a mechanism for the central bank to manage liquidity in the banking system.
  • By influencing the cost of borrowing and the return on deposits for banks, the LAF indirectly impacts short-term interest rates in the economy.
  • The goal is to maintain price stability, control inflation, and support overall economic objectives.

questions.question: Which monetary policy tool is complementary to Open Market Operations in achieving the objectives of the RBI?
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'A' that is 'Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)'.
  • Both Open Market Operations (OMOs) and the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) are instruments of monetary policy employed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to manage the money supply and liquidity in the economy.

Key Info: 

  • OMOs directly involve the buying and selling of government securities to inject or withdraw liquidity, while CRR influences the amount of funds available with banks for lending by mandating a portion of deposits to be held as reserves with the RBI.
  • The RBI can use these tools in tandem to control interest rates, influence credit availability, and achieve objectives like price stability and economic growth.

Additional info: 

  • Fiscal policy involves government spending and taxation decisions, which are distinct from monetary policy tools handled by the central bank.
  • FDI refers to investment made by a company or individual in one country into business interests in another country, and while influenced by monetary policy, it is not a tool itself.
  • GST is an indirect tax system aimed at simplifying taxation and improving the efficiency of the tax structure. It is part of fiscal policy, not monetary policy.
  • Agricultural subsidies: Agricultural subsidies are government incentives provided to farmers, falling under fiscal policy, and are not a tool of monetary policy.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the Repo Rate set by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI)?
questions.explanation:
• The primary purpose of the Repo Rate set by the RBI is to control inflation and influence short-term interest rates in the economy.
  • It is the rate at which banks borrow funds from the central bank by pledging government securities.
  • It plays a vital role in the central bank's overall monetary policy framework to achieve macroeconomic stability and economic growth.
  • The term "Repo" stands for Repurchase Agreement. In a Repo transaction, the RBI buys government securities from banks with an agreement to sell them back at a later date.
  • When the RBI lowers the Repo Rate, it becomes cheaper for banks to borrow money from the central bank against collateral (government securities). This encourages banks to borrow funds from the RBI, leading to an increase in liquidity in the banking system.

questions.question: Which of the following rates is applicable on the export credit refinance?
questions.explanation:
• The RBI, under Section 17(3A) of the RBI Act 1934, offers export credit refinance facilities to the scheduled banks.
  • At present, the credit refinance is offered up to 15% of the outstanding export credit. The rate applicable on the export credit refinance is the repo rate.
  • One can apply for an export credit refinance of Rs. 1 lakh and multiple thereof.

questions.question: Which of the following instruments is used in the LAF to inject liquidity into the banking system?
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'C' that is 'Repo Rate'.
  • In the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF), the RBI uses Repo (Repurchase Agreement) to inject liquidity into the banking system.
  • Banks can borrow funds from the RBI by pledging government securities.

Key Info: 

  • When a bank needs short-term liquidity, it can borrow money from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) by selling them government securities and then buying them back at a later date at a slightly higher price. 
  • This transaction is called a repurchase agreement (repo), and the interest rate associated with it is the repo rate.

Additional Info: 

  • A reverse repo is the opposite of a repo. In this scenario, the RBI buys securities from banks, effectively absorbing liquidity from the system.
  • While treasury bills are government securities, they are not directly used to inject liquidity through the LAF. 
  • The RBI might use treasury bills in other operations to manage liquidity, but the LAF primarily utilizes the repo mechanism.
  • Government securities are the asset used in repo transactions, but the term "government securities" itself doesn't represent the injection mechanism. The repo rate is the key element.
  • Call money is a very short-term loan between banks, typically used to meet immediate liquidity needs. While it can be related to liquidity management, it is not the primary instrument used within the LAF.

questions.question: The Reserve Bank of India was constituted which Committee to get recommendations and suggestions for improving the Monetary Policy Framework?
questions.explanation:
• The Urjit Patel committee was formed to get recommendations and suggestions for improving the Monetary Policy Framework.
  • Some recommendations made by the committee were:
  1. The nominal anchor for monetary policy should be the headline Consumer Price Index.
  2. The fiscal deficit is to be reduced to 3.0% of GDP by 2016-17.
  3. Monetary policy decisions should be vested in a Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), comprising the Governor, the Deputy Governor and Executive Director and two external full-time members.

questions.question: What does Repo Rate mean?
options: The interest rate at which the RBI lends to commercial banks instead of using government securities
The clients' interest rate on loans from commercial banks
It is a percentage of bank deposits that they keep with the RBI as Gold deposits only
It is a deposit made by banks with RBI in form of reserve or balances
questions.explanation:
• Repo rate is the rate at which RBI lends to its clients generally against government securities.
  • Repo rate is the interest rate at which the RBI lends to banks in the country.
  • The repo rate increases are intended to make credit costlier; banks generally pass on the increased costs to customers and loans become costlier.
  • Expensive credit dampens consumer demand, resulting in a corresponding drop in demand for goods and services.

questions.question: The Special Refinance Facility of the RBI was introduced under which section of the RBI Act?
questions.explanation:
• Refinance facilities are sector-specific and are given by the RBI to banks. Various types of refinance are offered by the RBI. Reserve Bank of India permitted the banks to offer to refinance on various loans like home, auto etc
  • A special refinance facility was introduced under Section 17(3B) of the RBI Act, 1934. This facility allows the scheduled commercial banks (except RRBs) to refinance up to 1% of Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL). The repo rate is applicable for this facility.

questions.question: The MSF, a monetary policy tool, refers to the facility under which scheduled commercial banks can borrow additional amount for _______ .
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'E' that is 'Overnight'.
  • The Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) is a monetary policy tool designed by the Resrrve Bank of India (RBI) to allow scheduled commercial banks to borrow a limited additional amount of funds when facing a severe liquidity shortage.
  • This borrowing is specifically for a very short duration, typically overnight.

Key Info:

  • The Reserve Bank of India, being a bankers’ bank, acts as a lender of last resort.
  • The Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) announced by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in its Monetary Policy, 2011-12. 
  • It acts as an emergency measure, enabling banks to access funds by dipping into their Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) holdings, up to a specified limit, at a penal interest rate.
  • The borrowing is allowed only overnight and up to 2% of the bank’s Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL).
  • The interest rate charged = Repo Rate + 0.25%.
  • Purpose: To act as a safety valve for banks during severe liquidity shortages.

questions.question: How does the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) differ from the Repo Rate in the context of borrowing by banks from the RBI?
options: MSF has a lower interest rate than Repo Rate
MSF has a higher interest rate than Repo Rate
MSF and Repo Rate are the same
questions.explanation:
• The Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) has a higher interest rate than the Repo Rate.
  • MSF provides a facility for banks to borrow funds at a higher rate in emergency situations when there is a severe shortage of liquidity.
  • It allows banks to borrow money from the central bank, which is typically secured by collateral such as government bonds or treasury bills.
  • The MSF is designed to be an inexpensive way for banks to access emergency funding, and is often used in response to sudden shocks in the inter-bank market or other unexpected liquidity pressure.
  • It's important to note that the use of MSF is closely monitored by financial regulators to ensure that it remains a reliable source of liquidity for banks in times of need.

questions.question: The RBI is required to publish a document called the Monetary Policy Report once every ______ months to explain the sources of inflation and the forecast of inflation for 6-18 months ahead.
questions.explanation:
• The RBI has to publish a document - Monetary Policy Report, once every 6 months to detail the sources of inflation and also forecast for inflation for the next 6-18 months.
  • Maintaining price stability while keeping in mind the objective of growth is the main objective of the Monetary Policy.

questions.question: In LAF, A stands for?
questions.explanation:
• LAF stands for Liquidity Adjustment Facility.

  • A liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) is a monetary policy tool used in India by the Reserve Bank of India or RBI.

  • The RBI introduced the LAF as part of the outcome of the Narasimham Committee on Banking Sector Reforms of 1998.

  • LAF's help the RBI manage liquidity and provide economic stability by offering banks the opportunity to borrow money through repurchase agreements or Repos or to make loans to the RBI via reverse repo agreements.

  • LAF’s can manage inflation in the economy by increasing and reducing the money supply.

questions.question: How many members are there in the monetary policy committee?
questions.explanation:
Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) was introduce in 2016 on the recommendation of Urjit Patel Committee. It is a 6 member committee in which 3 members are from RBI and 3 members are from Government of India. It was introduced with the motive to control the rate of inflation  through various tools. MPC had to maintain the rate of inflation in between 2%  to 6%.

Background-  In 2014, PM MODI announced to bring Indian Financial Court comprising of 7 members  (3 from RBI + 4 from Government of India) but former RBI Governor, Raguram Rajan had opposed it. So as a solution the MPC was formulated.

questions.question: Which of the following monetary policy objectives explains that the RBI provide sufficient credit for the increasing needs of the different sectors of the economy?
questions.explanation:
• Traditionally, the monetary policy in India was focused on controlling inflation.
  • This was done through the contraction of money supply and credit.
  • However, this resulted in poor growth of the economy.
  • Therefore, RBI adopted a new policy of growth with stability.
  • In simple terms, this means that the RBI will provide sufficient credit for the increasing needs of the different sectors of the economy.
  • Also, it will control inflation within a certain limit.

questions.question: In which year did the Government of India amend the RBI Act to establish the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) to set?
questions.explanation:
• In 2016, the RBI Act was amended by the Government of India to set up the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC).
  • The MPC membership is divided evenly between members of RBI and independent members appointed by the government. Thus, the role of RBI in setting up the interest rates was reduced.
  • The vote of the RBI governor is decisive, however, in case of a tie.

questions.question: Which component of NDTL is influenced by the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)?
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is (b) Time Liabilities.
  • SLR mandates banks to maintain a certain percentage of their time liabilities in the form of liquid assets like government securities.
  • Every bank must have a particular portion of their Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) in the form of cash, gold, or other liquid assets by the end of the day.
  • The ratio of these liquid assets to the demand and time liabilities is called the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR). The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has the authority to increase this ratio by up to 40%.

questions.question: What is the role of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) in India?
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'B' that is Formulating monetary policy.
  • The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) is an independent body in India responsible for formulating monetary policy to achieve macroeconomic stability.
  • It aims to control inflation, promote economic growth, and maintain financial stability.
  • The MPC, comprised of six members appointed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and one external member, meets eight times a year to review the monetary policy and make decisions on interest rates and quantitative measures.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) & Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR).

1. CRR helps in securing monetary stability and managing liquidity in the economy.

2. RBI can change the CRR to any level without any floor or ceiling limit

3. The maximum limit for SLR is 40%

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'E' that is 'All 1, 2 and 3'
  • CRR is a tool used by the central bank (RBI in India) to control the amount of funds available for banks to lend, thus influencing liquidity and maintaining financial stability.
  • The RBI Act was amended in 2006, removing the previous floor and ceiling limits for CRR, allowing the RBI to adjust it freely based on economic conditions.
  • RBI has kept 40% as the maximum limit for SLR.
  • On the other hand, the minimum limit of SLR is 0.

Key Info: 

  • In terms of Section 42(1) of the RBI Act, 1934 the Reserve Bank, having regard to the need to secure monetary stability in the country prescribe the CRR for Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs) without any floor or ceiling rate.
  • The other purpose of CRR is to manage liquidity (RBI can increase CRR to decrease liquidity in the economy) and it also ensures that a part of the bank’s deposit is with the Central Bank and is hence, safe.
  • As a depositor, the CRR and SLR requirements ensure that some of the deposits with Indian banks remain secure, even if banks make poor lending decisions.
  • In the absence of the CRR and SLR requirements, to make more profits banks may lend most of the deposits and if there is a sudden rush to withdraw, banks will struggle to meet the repayments to the depositors.

questions.question: A situation in which the rate of inflation slows down temporarily is known as _____.
questions.explanation:
• The term disinflation is used to refer to a situation when the rate of inflation slows down for a temporary period of time. In other words, it is used for the falling inflation rate.

  • For example, if the inflation rate falls from 5% to 2%, the situation is known as disinflation.

questions.question: The rate at which the RBI lends money to commercial banks for a short term (a maximum of 90 days) is called:
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'D' that is 'Repo rate'.
  • Repo stands for "Repurchase Agreement" rate.
  • It's the interest rate at which the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) lends money to commercial banks for short-term borrowing when they face a liquidity crunch.

Key Info: 

  • At Repo rate RBI lends short-term funds (up to 90 days) to commercial banks against the collateral of government securities.
  • It is used for injecting liquidity into the banking system.
  • It sis also known as the benchmark interest rat
  • If RBI follows a contractionary monetary policy, it increases the repo rate, which makes it expensive for commercial banks to borrow.
  • Similarly, if RBI follows an expansionary fiscal policy, it reduces the repo rate.

Additional Info: 

  • Reverse repo rate is the opposite of the repo rate. It's the rate at which commercial banks lend money to the RBI, essentially earning interest by depositing excess funds with the central bank.
  • While sometimes used interchangeably, "lending rate" can refer to various interest rates banks charge their customers for loans, including the base lending rate which is influenced by the repo rate.
  • Historically, "bank rate" was used to describe the rate at which the central bank lent to commercial banks. 
  • However, in modern usage, the term "repo rate" has largely superseded "bank rate".

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding Net demand and time liabilities of bank (NDTL):

  1. Current account, saving account deposits
  2. Fixed deposits cash certificates
  3. Interest accrued on deposits, unpaid dividend
  4. Paid up capital, reserves, any credit balance in the Profit & Loss Account of the bank

Which of the above are included in Net demand and time liabilities of bank (NDTL)?
questions.explanation:
Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) in India represent the aggregate of a bank's demand and time liabilities, with certain adjustments. Here's a breakdown of what is typically included in NDTL:

  1. Demand Deposits: These are funds that can be withdrawn by the account holder on-demand without any notice. Examples include current account deposits and demand liabilities portion of savings bank deposits.
  2. Time Liabilities: Time Deposits: These are deposits with a specific maturity period and include fixed deposits, recurring deposits, and any other deposit that is payable at the end of a specified period.
  3. Other Demand and Time Liabilities: It encompass various miscellaneous liabilities not included in the previously mentioned types of liabilities. These may include interest accrued on deposits, unpaid dividends, suspense account balances reflecting amounts owed to other banks or the public, participation certificates issued to other banks, cash collaterals, and similar items.

questions.question:
Match the following monetary policy tools with their descriptions:

COLUMN 1 COLUMN 2
1. Repo Rate A. Percentage of deposits banks must invest in government securities
2. Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) B. Interest rate at which RBI lends to commercial banks
3. Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) C. Percentage of deposits banks must hold with RBI

Select the option with correct matching pairs below.
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'D' that is '1-B, 2-C, 3-A'.
  • Repo Rate (1) is the interest rate at which RBI lends to commercial banks. This rate is used by the central bank to control liquidity and influence the economy's overall interest rates.
  • Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) (2) is the percentage of deposits banks must hold with RBI. It is a regulatory measure to ensure that banks have sufficient reserves and liquidity.
  • Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) (3) is the percentage of deposits banks must invest in government securities. This tool ensures that banks invest a portion of their funds in government-backed assets, contributing to the financial stability of the economy.
  • Understanding these tools and their functions helps in grasping how central banks manage monetary policy and influence economic conditions.

questions.question: The RBI is required to publish a document called the Monetary Policy Report once every ______ months to explain the sources of inflation and the forecast of inflation for 6-18 months ahead.
questions.explanation:
• The RBI has to publish a document - Monetary Policy Report, once every 6 months to detail the sources of inflation and also forecast for inflation for the next 6-18 months.

  • Maintaining price stability while keeping in mind the objective of growth is the main objective of the Monetary Policy.

questions.question: Which of the following statements  best describes the Direct Instrument of Monetary Policy?
options: Refers to the use of government spending and tax policies to influence economic conditions, especially macroeconomic conditions.
Measures employed by governments to stabilize the economy, specifically by       manipulating the levels and allocations of taxes and government expenditures.
Those instruments of monetary policy which enable the RBI to hit the monetary policy target (money supply, liquidity) without significant policy action by others.
Instruments of the RBI where policy actions/responses from institutions like commercial banks are also necessary for hitting the targets and objectives set by the RBI.
questions.explanation: • Direct instruments are those instruments of monetary policy which enable the RBI to hit the monetary policy target (money supply, liquidity) without significant policy action by others.

questions.question:
Which among the following is/are tasks of Monetary Policy Committee?

  1. Devise policy rate while maintaining price stability
  2. Fixing the benchmark policy rate (repo rate)
  3. Containing inflation within the specified target level
  4. Devising mechanism for implementing fiscal policy

Select the correct answer from following options:
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option C, that is only 1, 2 and 3 are tasks of Monetary Policy Committee.
  • The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of the RBI is responsible for formulating monetary policy to maintain price stability and ensure economic growth.

MPCs main tasks include:

  1. Devise policy rate while maintaining price stability – Yes. The MPC considers inflation and growth while recommending policy rates.

  2. Fixing the benchmark policy rate (repo rate) – Yes. The MPC decides the repo rate, which is the key policy rate for liquidity management.

  3. Containing inflation within the specified target level – Yes. The MPC is mandated to keep inflation within the target range notified by the Government of India.

  4. Devising mechanism for implementing fiscal policy – No. Fiscal policy (taxes, government expenditure, borrowing) is under the purview of the Finance Ministry, not the MPC.

Key point: MPC focuses on monetary policy (liquidity, interest rates, inflation), not fiscal policy.

questions.question: Which of the following is/are the Direct Instrument of Monetary Policy?
questions.explanation:
• The direct instruments are:
  • The Cash Reserve Ratio is the proportion of demand and time deposits (Net Demand and Time Liabilities) that every scheduled commercial bank has to keep with the RBI as cash reserves.
  • Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) is a requirement that commercial banks have to keep a certain proportion of their demand and time deposits as liquid assets in their vault. In the context of SLR, liquid assets mean assets in the form of cash, gold and approved securities (government securities).
  • Refinance facilities are sector-specific refinance facilities given by the RBI to banks. The main types of refinance facilities are those given to the export sector through banks. Export refinance facilities include foreign exchange, swap facility etc., offered by the RBI.

questions.question: The RBI is required to publish a document called the Monetary Policy Report once every __________ months to explain the sources of inflation and the forecast of inflation for 6-18 months ahead.
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'E' that is '6'.
  • As per the RBI Act, 1934 (amended in 2016), the Reserve Bank of India is required to publish a Monetary Policy Report (MPR) once every 6 months.

Purpose of MPR:

  • To explain the sources of inflation.
  • To provide the forecast of inflation for the next 6–18 months.
  • To ensure transparency and accountability of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC).

Key Info:

  • Monetary policy is the process by which the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) manages the supply of money, credit, and interest rates in the economy to achieve specific economic objectives.
  • Its main goals are price stability (controlling inflation), economic growth, and financial stability.
  • By regulating the money supply, RBI influences spending, investment, and overall economic activity.

Important tool for Monetary Policy:

  • Repo rate: Rate at which RBI lends to banks (short-term).
  • Reverse repo rate: Rate at which RBI borrows from banks.
  • CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio): % of deposits banks must keep with RBI.
  • SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio): % of deposits banks must keep in approved government securities.
  • Bank rate: Long-term lending rate by RBI.
  • Monetary policy can be tight (contractionary) or loose (expansionary) depending on economic conditions.

questions.question: What is the significance of the Reverse Repo rate in the LAF mechanism?
options: It is the rate at which banks borrow from the RBI
It is the rate at which banks lend to the RBI
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is 'B' that is 'It is the rate at which banks lend to the RBI'.
  • The Reverse Repo rate is a crucial tool used by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) within the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) mechanism. 
  • Under the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF), the Reverse Repo Rate is the interest rate at which the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) borrows money from commercial banks.
  • When banks have excess liquidity (surplus funds), they can lend these funds to the RBI at the reverse repo rate. 
  • It is a vital tool used by the RBI to manage liquidity, stabilize the economy, and regulate the flow of funds in the financial system.

Key Info: 

  • The Reverse Repo rate is a key component of the LAF mechanism. The LAF is designed to manage liquidity in the banking system, and the reverse repo rate plays a direct role in achieving this by absorbing excess liquidity. 
  • The rate at which banks borrow from the RBI is the repo rate, not the reverse repo rate.
  • The repo rate is when the RBI lends money to banks, while the reverse repo is when banks lend money to the RBI. 
  • While the reverse repo rate can indirectly influence inflation by managing liquidity, it's not the direct determinant.
  • The RBI uses a combination of tools, including the repo rate and other policy measures, to control inflation.
  • The reverse repo rate is a monetary policy tool used to manage liquidity and inflation. It has no direct impact on the fiscal deficit, which is the difference between government spending and revenue.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a money market instrument?
questions.explanation:
• The money market instruments are Treasury bills, commercial papers, certificates of deposits, and call money. It is highly liquid as it has instruments that have a maturity below one year.

  • Fixed deposit is a safe investment option that guarantees consistent interest rates, special interest rates for senior citizens, various interest payment options, and no market-related risks, with income tax deductions.

questions.question: How does the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) contribute to monetary policy implementation by the RBI?
options: It helps in managing short-term interest rates
questions.explanation:
• The Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) helps the RBI in managing short-term interest rates by providing a facility for banks to borrow funds in situations of severe liquidity shortage.
  • It is part of the overall framework of monetary policy implementation.
  • It allows banks to borrow money from the central bank, which is typically secured by collateral such as government bonds or treasury bills.
  • The MSF is designed to be an inexpensive way for banks to access emergency funding, and is often used in response to sudden shocks in the inter-bank market or other unexpected liquidity pressure.
  • It's important to note that the use of MSF is closely monitored by financial regulators to ensure that it remains a reliable source of liquidity for banks in times of need.

questions.question: How does an increase in the Repo Rate affect the economy?
options: Increases borrowing costs and may lead to a decrease in inflation
Lowers borrowing costs and stimulates economic growth
Has no impact on borrowing costs or inflation
questions.explanation:
• An increase in the Repo Rate raises the cost of borrowing for banks, leading to higher interest rates in the economy.
  • This tends to decrease inflation but may also slow down economic growth as borrowing becomes more expensive.
  • Higher Repo Rates make it more expensive for banks to borrow money from the central bank. This increase in the cost of borrowing is likely to be passed on to consumers and businesses in the form of higher interest rates on loans.
  • Individuals and businesses will face increased costs for various types of loans, including home loans, car loans, and business loans.
